title: The dinosaurs that never died
text: Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometres wide crashed into what is now Mexico. The impact caused fires, tsunamis and years of darkness, and around three quarters of all species on Earth disappeared. Among them, as every schoolchild knows, were the dinosaurs. Or were they? According to most palaeontologists today, one group of dinosaurs survived the disaster, and its descendants are still all around us. You may even have eaten one for lunch.

The idea that birds are living dinosaurs is not as new as it sounds. In 1861, just two years after Charles Darwin published his theory of evolution, workers in a quarry in Germany found the fossil of a strange creature. It had teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail like a reptile, but it also had clear feathers. They called it Archaeopteryx, and it immediately became famous as a possible link between reptiles and birds.

For more than a century, however, the connection remained controversial. Many experts believed that birds had developed from some other group of reptiles, and dinosaurs were generally imagined as slow, cold-blooded giants that had little in common with a sparrow. That image began to change in the nineteen sixties and seventies, when researchers studying a small, fast predator called Deinonychus noticed how similar its skeleton was to that of a bird.

The most convincing evidence, though, came from China. In 1996, farmers in the province of Liaoning discovered a small dinosaur whose body was covered in a fine layer of fuzzy filaments, an early form of feathers. Over the following years, the same region produced dozens of other feathered dinosaurs, preserved in extraordinary detail by volcanic ash. One of them, Yutyrannus, was a relative of Tyrannosaurus rex, which suggests that even some large meat eaters may have been at least partly covered in feathers.

These discoveries have transformed the way dinosaurs are pictured. The famous Velociraptor, shown in films as a scaly monster the size of a man, was in reality about as big as a turkey and almost certainly had feathers. Scientists have also found that many dinosaurs laid eggs in nests, sat on them to keep them warm and had lungs and bones similar to those of modern birds.

Why did feathers appear in the first place? Interestingly, it seems they did not evolve for flying. The earliest feathers were probably used to keep warm or to attract a partner, in the same way that a peacock shows off its tail. Only later did some small dinosaurs begin to use them to glide and eventually to fly.

So when you next see a pigeon in the park or a chicken on a farm, it is worth remembering their family history. The dinosaurs did not completely vanish when the asteroid hit. Some of them simply became smaller, grew wings and took to the skies.

parts.help: Write one word in each gap.
parts.text: Not all dinosaurs were giants. In fact, many of them were no bigger {{6}} a chicken.
